 Climate and human activities reshape Europe's flood and drought hazards 
 Climate and human activities reshape Europe's flood and drought hazards 
 While the climate frames Europe's broad hydrological trends, human activities such as urbanisation, dam construction, and water consumption play a decisive role in altering the scale of floods and droughts at local level.
 General publications
 26 October 2026
 Joint Research Centre
 3 min read
 © EU 
 Summary
 Climate change has, on average, increased floods in Europe by 0.5% and decreased droughts by 6.6%.
 Local impacts vary substantially, because of both regional climate dynamics and human activity.
 New research reveals the extent of shifting trends in floods and droughts across Europe over a period of seven decades. On average, climate change and variability contributed to a 0.5% rise in flood magnitude and a 6.6% drop in drought magnitude across Europe. However, these continental averages mask significant local variations driven by socio-economic factors.
 The study, co-authored by the JRC, the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK), the University of Szczecin and the University of Bologna, disentangles the individual impacts of climate, land use, reservoirs construction, and water use on Europe’s water extremes between 1951 and 2020. The results can support plans to improve resilience to floods and droughts, a key pillar of the  European Water Resilience Strategy .
 Regional climate dynamics 
 Since the 1950s, changing climate has created distinct regional hydrological trajectories across Europe
 currently, Europe’s continental and Atlantic regions are experiencing a ‘wetting’ trend, marked by increased flood severity and reduced drought severity
 the Mediterranean region is suffering a ‘drying’ trend, leading to intensified and prolonged droughts
 the Alpine, mountainous regions are facing hydrological ‘acceleration’, where shifting snowpack and precipitation patterns increase the severity of both floods and droughts
 in the Baltics and Scandinavia however, the trends show a slowdown of the intensity of droughts and floods.
 How human activity reshapes local hazards
 Socio-economic developments since 1950s have impacted the severity of floods and droughts locally, currently affecting 35% of the European river network. 
 Land use and urbanisation, expanding cities and sealed surfaces prevent water infiltration, accelerating runoff and worsening local flood peaks. Simultaneously, reforestation increases overall forest water uptake, which can lower river flows during dry spells.
 The construction of hundreds of dams and reservoirs has affected 13% of the European river network. They act as stabilisers by reducing the severity of both floods and droughts. However, increased surface evaporation from large reservoirs reduces the total overall river volume.
 Rising water demand also has an impact. Expanding water consumption, especially for domestic use, has intensified drought conditions in 10% of the river network. Domestic demand has steadily increased, becoming the largest water-use sector by 2020.

 Human activities
Driving consistent local trajectories --- 35% (River network changed)
 Land use change 27% (River network changed - Changes in land cover, such as growing cities) ↑ floods ↑ droughts
 Reservoirs construction 13% (River network changed - Store water and even out river flows) ↓ floods ↓ droughts
 Water demand changes 10% (River network changed - More water taken from rivers) - floods ↑ droughts
 Background
 The European Water Resilience Strategy aims to restore and protect the water cycle, including resilience against floods, droughts and water scarcity, improve water efficiency and secure clean and affordable water for all. By separating the influence of climate from that of land use, reservoirs and water consumption, this study shows where local pressures shape flood and drought hazards, helping authorities target measures where they will have the most effect. 
 The JRC also analyses climate change and its impact within the  PESETA programme . The objective is to understand and assess a wide range of climate risks in Europe, among them risks to agriculture, energy, and water resources, and the associated socio-economic impact. 
 The PESETA programme has run since 2006 in support of European policymaking on climate mitigation and adaptation.
